function.name: requests_get
function.description: Send a GET request to a specified URL to retrieve all products and branches with triangulation runs in the latest 90 days. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to send the GET request to.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The MIME types that are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request as a dictionary of header names to header values.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

days.description: The number of days to look back for triangulation runs.

end_date.description: The end date for the data retrieval period, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If null, defaults to the current date.

params.description: Optional query parameters to include in the request.

auth.description: HTTP authentication credentials as a (username, password) tuple.

cert.description: Path to a certificate file to verify the peer.

cookies.description: Cookies to send with the request as a dictionary of cookie names to cookie values.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: Proxy settings as a dictionary mapping protocol names to URLs of the proxies.

stream.description: If true, the response should be streamed; otherwise, the response will be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not.

message.content:
### What “triangulation metrics” usually mean In most data‑processing or GIS contexts, **triangulation** refers to the process of dividing a set of points (or a surface) into a mesh of triangles. The *metrics* that accompany a triangulation run are the quantitative descriptors that tell you how the mesh turned out and how the run performed. They are useful for: | Category | Typical metric | Why it matters | |----------|----------------|----------------| | **Mesh quality** | • **Number of triangles**
• **Average triangle area**
• **Minimum/maximum area**
• **Aspect ratio**
• **Minimum angle** | Indicates how fine or coarse the mesh is and whether triangles are well‑shaped (important for numerical stability). | | **Geometric fidelity** | • **Surface area error** (difference between triangulated surface and ground truth)
• **Hausdorff distance**
• **Mean squared error** | Measures how accurately the mesh represents the underlying geometry. | | **Computational performance** | • **Runtime**
• **Memory usage**
• **Number of iterations** (for iterative algorithms) | Helps optimize the algorithm or hardware. | | **Data provenance** | • **Input point count**
• **Timestamp**
• **Branch / product ID** | Useful for audit trails and reproducibility. | --- ### How the API’s `requests_get` function ties into this The function you mentioned: ```python requests_get( url="https://api.example.com/triangulation", params={"days": 90, "end_date": None} ) ``` is designed to pull **all products and branches that had triangulation runs in the last 90 days**. The JSON payload it returns typically contains entries like: ```json { "product_id": "P123", "branch_id": "B456", "run_id": "R789", "metrics": { "num_triangles": 15234, "avg_area": 0.0042, "min_angle": 15.3, "runtime_seconds": 42.7, "error_mean_squared": 0.00012 }, "timestamp": "2026-09-28T14:32:00Z" } ``` Each `metrics` block is a snapshot of the triangulation run’s performance and quality. By aggregating these over time, you can: 1. **Track trends** – e.g., is the average triangle area shrinking as more data points are added? 2. **Detect anomalies** – e.g., a sudden spike in runtime might indicate a bug or a hardware issue. 3. **Benchmark** – compare different algorithms or parameter settings across branches. --- ### Quick checklist for interpreting triangulation metrics | Metric | What to look for | Typical thresholds (example) | |--------|------------------|------------------------------| | **Num triangles** | Too few → under‑resolved; too many → over‑resolved | Depends on domain size | | **Avg area** | Smaller → finer mesh | < 0.01 m² for high‑res terrain | | **Min angle** | < 20° → skinny triangles → numerical instability | > 30° recommended | | **Aspect ratio** | > 5 → elongated triangles | < 3 preferred | | **Runtime** | Exceeds expected window | < 60 s for 10k points | | **Error metrics** | > threshold → poor fit | < 0.001 for most applications | --- ### Bottom line Triangulation metrics are the quantitative fingerprints of a mesh‑generation run. They let you assess **quality**, **accuracy**, and **performance** in a single, machine‑readable snapshot. The `requests_get` function you’re using simply fetches those snapshots for the last 90 days, so you can feed them into dashboards, alerts, or automated quality‑control pipelines.
